To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
consumption of a high protein meal vs. high carbohydrate meal does not influence the stress-induced cortisol and psychological response in men and women.
consumption of a high-carbohydrated meal does not affect physiological cortisol levels or psychological mood state, and that men show higher cortisol levels compared with women.
consumption of high-protein vs high-carbohydrate meals does not influence the stress-induced salivary and psychological mood response in men and women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of macronutrients on physiological cortisol and psychological mood response in men and women.
the effect of macronutrient composition of meals on the physiological and psychological mood response in men and women.
the effects of macronutrient composition of meals on the physiological and psychological stress response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the physiological and psychological stress-response is not influenced by consumption of meals with different carbohydrate and protein contents, and that men show a higher cortisol response compared with premenopausal women.

consumption of a high protein vs. high carbohydrate meal does not influence the stress-induced cortisol response in men and women, however men show a higher meal induced cortisol response compared to women.
the consumption of a high protein meal does not influence the psychological mood state, but it does influence the physiological cortisol response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a meal with a high protein content is not more stress-protective than a meal with a higher carbohydrate content.
a high protein meal does not affect the stress-induced cortisol response and psychological stress response compared to a high carbohydrate meal.
consumption of a high-carbohydrates meal does not induce a higher cortisol and psychological response compared with a high-protein diet.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the macronutrient composition of the meal does not influence the cortisol response, which was not expected, but the sex of the individual does.
a high-protein breakfast is not superior to a high-carbohydrates breakfast in terms of mood and physiological response.
the macronutrient content of the test-meal does not influence the meal-induced cortisol response, and that the cortisol response to meals differs between men and women.
